The background-check deadline fell at the same time as the cuts, but it applied identically everywhere, almost all lapsed volunteers held current checks, and deactivations were reversed. The site contrasts (C2) plus the mechanism, dose-response and rival exclusion in C7 justify committing to it. It is also cheap, targeted and reversible. With the initial file alone, the evidence would be insufficient."}],"discriminatingReads":["C2","C7"],"lowValueReads":["C1","C3","C4","C5","C8","C9","C10","C13","C15"],"optimalReadPath":["C2","C7"],"authoringNotes":"From the initial file alone, a careful analyst most likely keys H2 (coordinator cuts alone) as supported or leading. The 1 May cut matches the start of the slide in E5, and Millbrook, the one site that kept its coordinator, is reportedly fine (E4). Alternatively the analyst leans on H4 because of the 1 May deactivations. E2 is a rollout plan, not a record of actual go-lives, so Quarry Lane's postponement is visible only in C2; that is the fair counter to the plan. Initial-only answers: H1 unknown or contradicted on an interested claim; H2 tempting; H3 unknown; H4 unknown; H5 contradicted on timing; R1/R2 unknown; R3 association or unknown; R4 association-only; A1 premature; A4 premature; SUFF insufficient. C2 uniquely settles H2 as contradicted (Quarry Lane contrast). C7 uniquely settles R1 and R2 as causal and A1 as preferred (mechanism, dose-response, free admin seat). C7 alone leaves H2 unresolved, and C2 alone leaves R2 unknown. C6 (high fill rates), C11 ('app' and 'staff not around' themes) and C12 (admin login handed to the regional manager) hint at the mechanism but settle nothing. Arithmetic: site columns sum to the E5 totals; 213 April regulars = 110+103; 123 lapsed = 114+9; 90 remaining + 14 new = 104 August. Callback categories sum to 61. Checked as a skeptical reviewer: A4 is not harmful (it would improve retention) and not premature (it does not rely on an unconfirmed hypothesis). R3 is contradicted on direct evidence against the link, not merely because a rival wins. R4 has association but no mechanism, and no evidence counts against it."}}

case.title: Larkspur Community Food Network: regular volunteers drifting away
case.setting: Larkspur Community Food Network is a fictional regional food-relief nonprofit with four pantry sites (Millbrook, Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane). It relies on about 420 regular volunteers who sort, pack and serve food, including an after-school meals programme for minors at every site. In spring 2026 it introduced a self-scheduling app (RotaWeave) and an annual background-check renewal. After losing a foundation grant, it also eliminated three site coordinator posts. Between March and August the number of active regular volunteers fell sharply, and the board meets on 30 September.
case.presentingRequest: The executive director wants an independent view of why regular volunteers have stopped coming and what Larkspur should do. She intends to recommend cancelling the RotaWeave contract at the 30 September board meeting unless the evidence points elsewhere.

initialEvidence.source: Mara Ellison, Executive Director, memo to reviewer, 2 September 2026
initialEvidence.text: Our active regular volunteers fell from 421 in March to 295 in August, the worst drop in our eleven years. I have personally taken about a dozen calls from long-serving volunteers who are furious about RotaWeave, the scheduling app we adopted this spring. At the 30 September board meeting I intend to recommend cancelling the RotaWeave contract and going back to the paper rosters that served us for a decade. One board member also thinks Commonplate Volunteers, a new group that opened on 16 June, is poaching our people. I need an independent view of what happened and what we should do before that meeting.

initialEvidence.source: Larkspur project and policy change log (extract)
initialEvidence.text: RotaWeave rollout plan (approved 12 Feb): Millbrook pilot go-live 3 March; Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane go-live 14 April. Basic tier: next week's shifts released to all volunteers every Thursday at 18:00; three staff admin seats; 3-year term, $38,000; early-termination fee $14,000. Policy change (adopted 20 Jan): annual background-check renewal for all regular volunteers, required by the county after-school meals contract and by our insurer for any shift serving minors. Renewal deadline 30 April; volunteers not renewed are deactivated on 1 May until they complete it.

After the loss of the Pellham Foundation operating grant ($171,000), the following savings take effect on 1 May. The site coordinator posts at Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane are eliminated (3.0 FTE, $148,000 annualised), and volunteer oversight at those three sites moves to the regional operations manager. The Millbrook coordinator post is kept because the county senior-meals contract funds it separately. The remaining savings come from reduced van leasing. We recognise this places extra load on site lead volunteers and thank them for their flexibility.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Tobias Wren, Director of Operations and sponsor of the RotaWeave project, to the Executive Director, 28 August 2026
initialEvidence.text: Mara, before the board blames RotaWeave, look at Millbrook. It has been on the app since March, longer than any other site, and its numbers are fine. The slide starts in May, not April. On 1 May we deactivated 23 regulars who hadn't finished their background-check renewal, and plenty more told me the renewal portal was a nightmare. I think the renewal drove people off whether or not they finished it. Cancelling RotaWeave would cost $14k and throw away the attendance data we've finally got for funders. Tobias

Definition: an active regular is a volunteer with 3 or more shifts in the prior 60 days. Org-wide month-end counts: Jan 409, Feb 414, Mar 421, Apr 415, May 384, Jun 345, Jul 315, Aug 295. Renewal deadline: 23 regulars were deactivated on 1 May for an incomplete background-check renewal. Of these, 21 completed it and were reactivated by 31 May; the other 2 have since moved away. Site-level counts are not part of the standard board pack.

initialEvidence.source: Volunteer pulse survey summary, February and June 2026
initialEvidence.text: Anonymous link sent to all regulars. Overall satisfaction (1–5): February mean 4.2 (n=236); June mean 3.5 (n=198). The lowest-scoring item in June was 'ease of getting the shifts I want' at 3.0, down from 4.1. Follow-up: 61 June respondents chose to give their names and were matched to activity records. Of those who scored overall satisfaction at 2 or below, 7 of 19 (37%) were inactive by August, against 4 of 42 (10%) of the rest. Site is not recorded.

Adoption: 92% of active volunteers at live sites logged in at least once in August. Account manager's note: 'Larkspur is one of our smoothest Basic-tier deployments. We'd welcome a conversation about Plus-tier features.'

catalogue.text: Basic tier has no recurring bookings, so a regular keeps a weekly slot only if staff book it before Thursday's public release. catalogue.title: Board minutes, 12 February 2026 (RotaWeave procurement)
catalogue.text: Item 4: the Director of Operations presented the RotaWeave proposal, comparing three vendors. The board chose the Basic tier on cost ($38,000 over three years, against $61,000 for Plus). hypotheses.text: The move to app-based self-scheduling, on its own, caused the fall in active regular volunteers.
The elimination of site coordinator posts, on its own, caused the fall in active regular volunteers.
The fall in active regular volunteers arose from the move to app-based self-scheduling and the elimination of site coordinator posts acting together; neither change on its own produces it.
The background-check renewal requirement, on its own, caused the fall in active regular volunteers.
Recruitment by the newly opened Commonplate Volunteers, on its own, caused the fall in active regular volunteers.

actions.text: At Dock Street and Westgate, give a staff member or trained lead volunteer a RotaWeave admin seat and the job of booking regulars into their usual weekly slots before each Thursday release. Phone lapsed regulars to offer them their former slot back, and review re-engagement after 60 days.
Make a volunteer recognition and appreciation programme the centrepiece of the retention response, on the premise that low satisfaction is what is driving regulars to leave.
Suspend the background-check renewal requirement until volunteer numbers recover.
Cancel the RotaWeave contract at all four sites, paying the $14,000 early-termination fee, and return to paper rosters.
Before the board meeting, remove regulars with no shift in the past 45 days from the volunteer roster and from the retention figures.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: Two changes acting together caused Larkspur's fall in active regulars. RotaWeave's Basic tier has no recurring bookings and releases next week's shifts to everyone each Thursday, so a regular keeps a usual weekly slot only if a staff admin books it beforehand. Coordinators did this ('book on behalf') at Millbrook from March, and at Dock Street and Westgate from 14 April. On 1 May the coordinator posts at Dock Street, Westgate and Quarry Lane were cut. At Dock Street and Westgate nobody took over the pre-booking, so regulars' slots went to new and corporate sign-ups. Of those who lost their slot, 88% lapsed, against 11% of those who kept it. Each change alone looks harmless because of a contrast site. Millbrook (app, coordinator kept) stayed stable. Quarry Lane (coordinator cut, app postponed, paper standing roster kept by a lead volunteer) also stayed stable. The background-check deadline fell at the same time as the cuts, but it applied identically everywhere, almost all lapsed volunteers held current checks, and deactivations were reversed. Commonplate opened after the decline began. Satisfaction fell over the same period, but there is no evidence that it caused volunteers to leave. The best response is to restore pre-booking of standing slots at the two affected sites and invite lapsed regulars back. Cancelling RotaWeave would probably also work, but it costs $14,000 and disrupts a site that is working.

answers.rationale: The executive director blames the app (E1). C2 confirms that Millbrook, on RotaWeave since March with its coordinator kept, held 118→111, and C7 shows only 7 of 117 Millbrook regulars lost their slot. Without the coordinator cut, the app did not produce the fall, so the app on its own is contradicted. E4 asserts the Millbrook figure, but E4 comes from the app's sponsor and is unverified until C2.

From the initial file alone, H2 looks strong: the cuts took effect on 1 May, the slide starts in May, and the only site that kept its coordinator is reportedly fine. Only C2 reveals that Quarry Lane never went live on RotaWeave and, despite losing its coordinator, stayed stable (86→80) on a paper standing roster. So the coordinator cut on its own does not produce the fall.

C2 gives the 2x2 contrast: app plus coordinator stable; coordinator cut without the app stable; app plus coordinator cut collapsed at both such sites, with the drop starting in May, after the coordinator cut rather than at April go-live. C7 supplies the mechanism. Basic tier has no recurring bookings, coordinators pre-booked regulars, pre-booking stopped on 1 May at Dock Street and Westgate, regulars lost their slots, and those who lost slots lapsed at 88% against 11%. No rival explains the site pattern.

The renewal deadline falls on the same date as the coordinator cuts (E2, E3), and the operations director, who sponsored the app, blames it (E4). But the requirement applied identically at all sites, and two sites were stable (C2). 121 of 123 lapsed volunteers held current checks (C7), no callback cited renewal, and 21 of 23 deactivations were reversed within May (E5).

The decline began in May (E5), before Commonplate opened on 16 June (E1). Only 2 of 61 lapsed regulars reached by callback had joined another group (C7), and the losses are confined to two sites with a specific change pattern (C2).

Temporal order: book-on-behalf entries at Dock Street and Westgate fell from 74 to 3 a week after 1 May, followed by slot losses in May–June (C7). Mechanism: there are no recurring bookings, slots are released publicly on Thursday, and new or corporate sign-ups took them. Contrast: Millbrook kept its coordinator and its pre-booking, and only 7 of 117 regulars lost their slot. C6's high fill rates are consistent with this, because the slots were filled by others.

In C7, 88% of regulars who lost their slot lapsed, against 11% of those who kept it. The slot loss followed an externally imposed stop to pre-booking rather than the volunteers' own drift. 44 of 61 callbacks name the lost shift, and the main rival (renewal) is ruled out because the lapsed volunteers held current checks.

The evidence counts against the link itself. The same deadline produced no fall at Millbrook or Quarry Lane (C2). The volunteers who lapsed held current checks (C7), and the deactivations were almost all reversed within May (E5). The only support is the coincidence of dates and an interested manager's opinion (E4).

In E6, low-satisfaction respondents were more often inactive by August (37% against 10%), so the two are associated. Nothing establishes that dissatisfaction itself drives lapse: there is no mechanism, the sample is small and self-selected, and losing a slot (C7) could produce both. Nothing counts against the link either, so it is neither causal nor contradicted.

This action restores the missing ingredient (pre-booking of standing slots) at exactly the two affected sites. Millbrook shows that it works inside RotaWeave (C7), an admin seat is free, the cost is low, it is reversible, and it includes outreach to recoverable lapsed regulars. It is better than A4.

This would help only if dissatisfaction were causing the lapses, a link that is merely associational (R4). Making it the main response ignores the slot-loss mechanism shown in C7. If the premise is wrong, recognition activity causes no lasting damage.

The checks are required by the county contract and the insurer for shifts serving minors (E2, C14). Suspending them disables a safeguarding control and puts the contract at risk. Under the supported explanation it would recover no volunteers, because the lapsed regulars already held current checks (C7).

Removing the app at Dock Street and Westgate would probably restore standing paper rosters, as at Quarry Lane (C2), so it would work under the supported joint explanation. It is not premature, because it does not depend on an unconfirmed hypothesis. It is not harmful either: it does not worsen outcomes or disable a control. But it costs $14,000 during a budget shortfall and disrupts Millbrook, which works fine (C7), so it is reasonable but inferior to A1.

This would flatter the retention figure before a board decision and drop recoverable regulars from the roster. C7 shows many lapsed regulars left only because they lost their slot. It suppresses information and worsens outcomes under every explanation.

The top-ranked substantive action is A1. The site contrasts (C2) plus the mechanism, dose-response and rival exclusion in C7 justify committing to it. It is also cheap, targeted and reversible. With the initial file alone, the evidence would be insufficient.

truth.authoringNotes: From the initial file alone, a careful analyst most likely keys H2 (coordinator cuts alone) as supported or leading. The 1 May cut matches the start of the slide in E5, and Millbrook, the one site that kept its coordinator, is reportedly fine (E4). Alternatively the analyst leans on H4 because of the 1 May deactivations. E2 is a rollout plan, not a record of actual go-lives, so Quarry Lane's postponement is visible only in C2; that is the fair counter to the plan. Initial-only answers: H1 unknown or contradicted on an interested claim; H2 tempting; H3 unknown; H4 unknown; H5 contradicted on timing; R1/R2 unknown; R3 association or unknown; R4 association-only; A1 premature; A4 premature; SUFF insufficient. C2 uniquely settles H2 as contradicted (Quarry Lane contrast). C7 uniquely settles R1 and R2 as causal and A1 as preferred (mechanism, dose-response, free admin seat). C7 alone leaves H2 unresolved, and C2 alone leaves R2 unknown. C6 (high fill rates), C11 ('app' and 'staff not around' themes) and C12 (admin login handed to the regional manager) hint at the mechanism but settle nothing. Arithmetic: site columns sum to the E5 totals; 213 April regulars = 110+103; 123 lapsed = 114+9; 90 remaining + 14 new = 104 August. Callback categories sum to 61. Checked as a skeptical reviewer: A4 is not harmful (it would improve retention) and not premature (it does not rely on an unconfirmed hypothesis). R3 is contradicted on direct evidence against the link, not merely because a rival wins. R4 has association but no mechanism, and no evidence counts against it.
